title: Moves no one should play
objectives: Remove dominated strategies until the game is small.

screens.title: Tight or wide
screens.prose: Two desks, Ana's and Ben's, each quote Tight or Wide to the same clients. Ana chooses the row and Ben the column. Each cell is (Ana's payoff, Ben's payoff), in £1,000 a day.
screens.question: Whatever Ben does, which quote earns Ana more?

options.why: You looked at (Wide, Wide), where both earn 4. Column by column, Tight pays Ana more: 2 > 1 and 5 > 4.
Check each column: Tight wins against Ben's Tight and against his Wide, so Ben's choice does not matter.

hints.text: Compare Ana's first numbers in one column, then the other.
Against Tight: 2 or 1. Against Wide: 5 or 4.
Tight wins both comparisons.

feedback.correct: Tight: 2 > 1 against Tight and 5 > 4 against Wide.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare Ana's payoffs in each column separately.

byKey.b: You picked the cell where both do well. Against each of Ben's quotes, Tight pays Ana more.

explain.text: Against Ben's Tight, Ana earns 2 by Tight and 1 by Wide. Against his Wide, 5 against 4. Tight is better whatever Ben does.

screens.title: Both quote tight
screens.prose: Tight beats Wide against every reply, so we say Wide is **strictly dominated** by Tight. The table is symmetric, so the same holds for Ben.
screens.question: Each desk plays its dominant quote. What does each earn a day, in £?

hints.text: Delete Wide for both desks. Which cell is left?
Only (Tight, Tight) survives.
That cell is (2, 2), in £1,000 a day.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the cell left once both desks drop Wide.

byKey.wide: £4,000 each is (Wide, Wide). Both would like it, but each gains by switching to Tight.
byKey.sucker: £5,000 needs the other desk to quote Wide, which it never does.
byKey.units: The table is in £1,000 a day, so 2 means £2,000.

explain.text: Both desks quote Tight and earn £2,000 a day each. Both quoting Wide would earn £4,000 each, yet neither stays there. This shape, where each one's best move leaves both worse off, is the **prisoner's dilemma**.

screens.title: Delete and look again
screens.prose: A bigger game, (Ana, Ben) in £. Delete one strictly dominated move at a time. After each deletion, look again: the smaller table can show a new one.
screens.question: Delete moves until one cell is left.

s0.tex: \text{Rows } T, M, B;\ \text{columns } L, C, R

ops.label: Delete Ana's B
ops.why: Against C, B pays 9, more than T's 5, so nothing dominates B yet.

ops.label: Delete Ana's M
ops.why: Against C, M pays 8, more than T's 5, so T does not beat M yet.

ops.label: Delete Ben's R
ops.why: In row B, R pays Ben 8, more than L's 0 and C's 6.

ops.label: Delete Ben's L
ops.why: In row T, L pays Ben 3, more than C's 1 and R's 2.

canvas.caption: C is gone: R paid Ben more in every row (2 > 1, 6 > 4, 8 > 6).

ops.label: Delete Ben's R
ops.why: R still pays Ben more than L in rows M and B: 6 > 1 and 8 > 0.

ops.label: Delete Ben's L
ops.why: In row T, L pays Ben 3, more than R's 2.

canvas.caption: M is gone: T beats it over L and R (4 > 2, 6 > 3).

ops.label: Delete Ben's R
ops.why: B is still in play, and there R pays Ben 8 against L's 0.

ops.label: Delete Ben's L
ops.why: In row T, L pays Ben 3, more than R's 2.

canvas.caption: B is gone: T beats it over L and R (4 > 3, 6 > 2).

ops.label: Delete Ben's R
ops.why: M is still in play, and there R pays Ben 6 against L's 1.

ops.label: Delete Ben's L
ops.why: In row T, L pays Ben 3, more than R's 2.

canvas.caption: Only row T is left for Ana.

ops.label: Delete Ben's L
ops.why: In row T, L pays Ben 3 and R pays 2, so L is the one to keep.

hints.text: At the start only one move is beaten everywhere. Check Ben's columns.
Compare Ben's C with his R, row by row: 1 < 2, 4 < 6, 6 < 8.
Delete C; then T beats M and B over L and R; then L beats R in row T.

feedback.correct: C, then M and B, then R: the game ends at (T, L) = (4, 3).
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep deleting until a single cell is left.

explain.text: First Ben's C goes, beaten by R in every row. Without C, T beats M and B for Ana. With only row T left, Ben prefers L (3) to R (2), so the game ends at (T, L).

screens.title: Beaten by a mix
screens.prose: Only Ana's payoffs are shown, in £. No single row beats D: U loses to it against R, and M loses to it against L. Ana may also toss a coin between two rows.
screens.question: Which plan strictly beats D against both of Ben's columns?

options.why: U pays 0 against R, less than D's 1.
You compared D with one row at a time. A mix of two rows can beat it where neither row can alone.
Against R that pays 0.5, less than D's 1.

hints.text: Try a coin toss between the two rows that each beat D somewhere.
U wins against L and M wins against R.
Half U, half M pays 1.5 against each column.

feedback.correct: Half U, half M pays 1.5 against L and 1.5 against R, more than D's 1 each time.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average two rows and compare the result with D in each column.

byKey.c: Each row alone fails somewhere, but their average pays 1.5 in both columns, more than D's 1.

explain.text: Half U and half M pays $\tfrac12(3) + \tfrac12(0) = 1.5$ against L and the same against R. D pays 1 against each. So D is strictly dominated by a mix and can go.

screens.title: What the mix pays
screens.prose: Check the coin toss in numbers. Ana plays U with chance $\tfrac12$ and M with chance $\tfrac12$.
screens.question: What does the mix pay Ana against L, in £?

hints.text: Weight each row's payoff against L by $\tfrac12$.
U pays 3 and M pays 0 against L.
$\tfrac12 \times 3 + \tfrac12 \times 0 = 1.5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average U's and M's payoffs against L.

byKey.u: That is U alone. The mix plays M half the time, which pays 0.
byKey.d: That is D's own payoff. The mix pays more.

explain.text: Against L the mix pays 1.5 and against R also 1.5. D pays 1 in both, so the mix beats it by 0.5 everywhere. The same check, with Ben's numbers, can remove one of his columns.

screens.title: Weakly beaten
screens.prose: U and D are never better than M for Ana, and sometimes worse. A candidate deletes them anyway. Order 1: delete U, then Ben's L. Order 2: delete D, then Ben's R.
screens.question: Do the two orders end at the same payoff?

options.text: Yes: deleting dominated moves never depends on the order
options.why: That holds for strict deletion. U and D only tie M in places, and with ties the order picks the answer.
Deleting D first and then R leaves column L, where U and M both pay (1, 1).

hints.text: Follow each order to the end.
Order 1 leaves column R, where M and D both pay (2, 1).
Order 2 leaves column L, where U and M both pay (1, 1).

feedback.correct: No: order 1 ends at (2, 1), order 2 at (1, 1).
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Play out each order and read the cells left.

byKey.b: You trusted that order never matters. That is true only when every deleted move is strictly beaten.

explain.text: In four cells, (U, L), (M, L), (M, R) and (D, R), neither player gains by moving alone. Weak deletion threw some of them away, and the order chose which. From here on we delete only **strictly** dominated moves.

canvas.caption: The four cells where neither player gains by moving alone.

screens.title: Nothing to delete
screens.prose: Matching pennies at £1: Ana and Ben each show Heads or Tails. Ana wins £1 from Ben when the coins match, and Ben wins £1 when they differ.
screens.question: Which moves can strict deletion remove?

options.why: Against Ben's Tails, Tails pays Ana 1 and Heads pays −1, so Heads does not beat it.
Against Ana's Tails, Heads pays Ben 1 and Tails pays −1, so Tails does not beat it.

hints.text: Is any move worse against every reply?
Each move wins against one reply and loses against the other.
So nothing is dominated.

feedback.correct: None: every move is best against something.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each move against both replies.

explain.text: Each move wins against one reply and loses against the other. So no move is dominated and deletion leaves the whole table. Lesson 4 solves this game another way.

screens.title: Strict dominance
screens.prose:
What you did: move $s$ is strictly dominated by move $t$ when $t$ pays more against every reply $c$. Delete it, then look again.

$$u(t, c) > u(s, c) \quad \text{for every } c$$
screens.question: One row pays Ana (4, 2, 7) against three columns, another (5, 3, 7). Is the first strictly dominated by the second?

options.text: No: they tie against the third column
Yes: the second row is never worse
options.why: Never worse is weak dominance. Strict needs more against every column, and 7 equals 7.

options.text: Yes: the second row wins in two of three columns
options.why: Strict dominance needs a win in every column, not most of them.

hints.text: Compare column by column.
A tie breaks strict dominance.

feedback.correct: No: a tie in one column means only weak dominance.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Strict means more in every column.

explain.text: The second row wins in two columns and ties in the third. That is weak dominance, which the trap showed is unsafe to delete. Strict dominance needs a strict win against every reply.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Three games, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the reasoning aloud before you answer. A round deletes every move that is strictly dominated at that point.
screens.question: Fill in the four answers.

rows: This game: what does Ana earn in the cell left?
This game: how many rounds of deletion?
The game you solved by deleting one move at a time: how many rounds?
Ben's payoffs: row T (4, 0, 1), row B (0, 4, 1) for L, C, R. What does half L, half C pay him in row T?

hints.text: In this game, compare T with M first.
T loses to M in every column: 1 < 7, 4 < 9, 0 < 5.
T goes; then R beats L and C; then B beats M in column R. Ana earns 6. The coin toss pays $\tfrac12(4 + 0) = 2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: Round 1 removes T. Round 2 removes L and C, since R pays Ben more in rows M and B. Round 3 removes M, leaving 6.
byKey.r1c1: Count rounds, not moves: T; then L and C together; then M.
byKey.r2c1: That game went C; then M and B together; then R: three rounds.
byKey.r3c1: Half of 4 and half of 0 is 2, which beats R's 1 in row T. Row B is the same.

explain.text: T goes first, then Ben's L and C, then M ($5 < 6$ in column R). The game ends at (B, R), Ana's payoff 6, in three rounds. The coin toss between L and C pays Ben 2 in each row, so his R is dominated.

screens.title: Follow-up: a third desk
screens.prose: Follow-up: the interviewer adds a third desk. A desk quoting Tight earns £3,000 a day plus £2,000 for each other desk quoting Wide. A desk quoting Wide earns £2,000 for each other desk quoting Wide.

state.caption: One desk's payoff a day, by how many of the other two quote Wide.

screens.question: Which quote should each desk choose?

options.text: Wide, since all Wide pays most
options.why: All Wide pays £4,000 each, but a desk that switches to Tight then earns £7,000.

options.text: It depends on how many others quote Wide
options.why: Fill one column at a time: Tight is £3,000 ahead in each, so the count does not matter.

hints.text: Fill each column of the table for one desk.
With $k$ others Wide, Tight pays $3000 + 2000k$ and Wide pays $2000k$.
Tight is always £3,000 better.

feedback.correct: Tight: it pays £3,000 more in every case.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two quotes for each number of other desks quoting Wide.

byKey.b: You looked at the best outcome for the group. Each desk alone gains £3,000 by switching to Tight.

explain.text: With $k$ others quoting Wide, Tight pays $3000 + 2000k$ and Wide pays $2000k$. Tight wins by £3,000 in every column, so it is strictly dominant. The third desk changes nothing about that.

screens.title: Follow-up: what they earn
screens.prose: All three desks follow their dominant quote. The table now shows one desk's payoff in each case.
screens.question: What does each desk earn a day, in £?

hints.text: Everyone quotes Tight, so how many others quote Wide?
Zero others Wide: the first column.
Tight with 0 others Wide pays £3,000.

feedback.correct: £3,000 each, against £4,000 if all quoted Wide.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. With every desk on Tight, read the column for 0 others Wide.

byKey.wide: £4,000 is what all Wide would pay. No desk stays there, since Tight pays £7,000 against two Wide desks.
byKey.best: £7,000 needs both other desks on Wide, which neither chooses.

explain.text: All three quote Tight and earn £3,000 each, though all Wide would pay £4,000 each. A quiet agreement to quote wide unravels, because each desk gains £3,000 a day by breaking it. The prisoner's dilemma survives a third player.

ideas: A move is strictly dominated when another move, or a mix of moves, pays more against every reply.
Delete it and look again: a smaller table can make a new move dominated.
Delete only strictly dominated moves; weak deletion can lose equilibria and depends on the order.

formula.name: Strict dominance
formula.tex: u(t, c) > u(s, c) \quad \text{for every } c

summary.trap: Deleting a move that only ties in places. The order of weak deletions can change the answer.

quiz.prose: Only Ben's payoffs are shown, in £. Ana chooses the row and Ben the column.
quiz.question: Which of Ben's columns is strictly dominated?

options.text: R, by half L and half C
None: each column is best somewhere
options.why: You compared R with L and with C one at a time. Half of each pays 2 in each row, more than R's 1.
L pays 4 in row T, more than C's 0, so C does not beat it.

feedback.correct: R: the coin toss between L and C pays 2 in each row, more than 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try a coin toss between two columns.

explain.text: Half L and half C pays $\tfrac12(4 + 0) = 2$ in row T and $\tfrac12(0 + 4) = 2$ in row B. R pays 1 in both. So R is strictly dominated by the mix.

quiz.prose: Ana chooses the row and Ben the column; each cell is (Ana's payoff, Ben's payoff), in £.
quiz.question: Delete strictly dominated moves. What does Ben earn in the cell left?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. T beats B for Ana and L beats R for Ben.

byKey.kept-b: You kept B for Ben's 3. B is beaten by T in both columns, 4 > 3 and 2 > 1.

explain.text: T beats B for Ana (4 > 3, 2 > 1) and L beats R for Ben (1 > 0, 3 > 2). Both go in one round. The cell left is (T, L) = (4, 1).

quiz.prose: Two funds each keep their fees or cut them. Each cell is (Ana's fund, Ben's fund), in £m a year.
quiz.question: Where do the two funds end up?

options.why: Both would prefer it, but Cut beats Keep for each fund against every reply.
The fund keeping its fees would switch to Cut and earn 1 instead of 0.

feedback.correct: Both cut: Cut is strictly dominant for each.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether one move beats the other against every reply.

explain.text: Cut pays 4 against Keep and 1 against Cut; Keep pays 3 and 0. So Cut strictly dominates Keep for both funds. They end at (1, 1), the prisoner's dilemma again.
